stories.summary: Africa: The Trade Pact That Could Stitch Africa's Textile Industry Together Bird Story Agency Garment manufacturing 30 August 2026 Bird Story Agency (Africa) By Muchemwa Mugadzaweta The AfCFTA offers African cotton, textile and clothing businesses the opportunity to build cross-border production networks, attract investment and retain more value on the continent. And it can do so while providing the shared rules and larger market needed to strengthen factories and trade corridors. More than five years after trading began under the African Continental Free Trade Area, one of its biggest tests is taking shape in the textile industry: can it connect the continent’s cotton growers, spinners, weavers and clothing manufacturers into a competitive regional production network? The AfCFTA offers access to a larger market and preferential trade, but its success will be measured by whether businesses can move African-made inputs across borders and turn that opportunity into factories, investment and jobs. stories.title: Humanitarian crisis worsening in refuge for civilians fleeing Sudan’s civil war
stories.summary: Save the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Save the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Humanitarian crisis worsening in refuge for civilians fleeing Sudan’s civil war Conditions are deteriorating in city of El Obeid and camps on its outskirts, with more people arriving every day Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside. The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children. “The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety. The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.” The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

stories.title: Turkish, Somali forces free vessel seized by pirates in Somalia
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5Jd4B Puntland Maritime Police Forces PMPF patrol against the pirate attacks off the coast in Puntland, Somalia [FILE: January 29, 2024] Image: Abuukar Mohamed Muhidin/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO Advertisement Turkey ’s navy and Somali armed forces have freed a hijacked vessel in Somali waters and killed 14 alleged pirates following a battle that lasted several days, Somalia ’s government said on Saturday. "During the 10-day operation, four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed," said a Somali Defense Ministry statement. "The sustained military pressure finally forced the remaining pirates to abandon the ship." The MV LUTUF, a Cameroon-flagged vessel, was hijacked on August 17 off the coast of the Nugaal region of Puntland state. The joint Turkey-Somalia operation was carried out as part of a defense cooperation agreement between the two countries. The ministry did not provide details about any casualties or the well-being of the crew aboard the vessel but said, "The forces subsequently secured the MV LATUF, which has now safely resumed its journey." According to AFP news agency sources, at least eight members of the crew were on board, including one Turkish national. Resurgence of piracy along Somalia’s coast The Horn of Africa has seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year. At least five cargo ships were held hostage, the most recent of which was seized on August 20 off Yemen.

stories.title: Uganda: Direct Sales Give Eastern Uganda's Cotton Farmers a Stronger Hand
stories.summary: Uganda: Direct Sales Give Eastern Uganda's Cotton Farmers a Stronger Hand Phoebe Masongole, Bird Story Agency Members of the Bukedea Cotton Farmers Association, cotton farmers, pose for a group photograph near their cotton garden in Bukedea District, Uganda, in July 2026. 29 August 2026 Bird Story Agency (Africa) By Phoebe Masongole Cotton farmers in eastern Uganda are bypassing village middlemen and selling collectively or directly to ginneries. The emerging model is giving growers greater control over weighing, payment and market access - and helping women turn seasonal cotton earnings into education, land, homes and productive assets. When Nighty Acen sold her cotton directly to Iki-Iki Cotton Ginnery in neighbouring Pallisa District, the change was about more than finding a buyer. It meant avoiding village middlemen who, she says, offered farmers low prices and sometimes used poorly maintained weighing scales. The income from cotton helped Acen build an iron-roofed house, contribute to her son’s marriage and buy oxen.

stories.title: Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pirates manage to board ships operating a long way from the coast and then guide them closer to the shore By Barbara Plett Usher Africa correspondent Published 29 August 2026 A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran. Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates. It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade. "Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity." That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north. Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz. Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father. The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US. "They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service. stories.title: Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Zolani Tete was in training for a comeback fight when he was killed By Khanyisile Ngcobo ,Â Reporting from Johannesburg Â and Â Jude Winter ,Â BBC Sport Published 24 August 2026 Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday. Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital. One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges. Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014.

Photograph: EvritFilms Review On Different Grounds review – Cupid’s-conspiracy romcom brings Nollywood and Bollywood together Mildred Okwo’s earnest film about the conflicting romantic wishes in a Nigerian family struggles to connect with its promising premise I t’s a stretch for this Nigerian romcom to bill itself “the first Nollywood-Bollywood collaboration” based on the fact that it features, in Nimesh Diliprai Desai and Vineet Raina, two fringe Indian players on a sprawling wedding-invite list. But the two industries do indeed have much common ground, such as big-hearted family values and a penchant for grand gestural emotions that, in the case of Mildred Okwo’s somewhat heavy-footed film, trample on some promising concepts and narrative plausibility. Silk-tressed bachelorette Aurora (Abena Akuaba) is being browbeaten by her businessman dad Eyimofe (Bob-Manuel Udokwu) to marry snoozefest suitor Tobore (Ifeanyi Kalu).

The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the ⁠site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash ⁠floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa .
